nameStory: The Garden Arion earns its name from being one of the most common slugs found munching through vegetable gardens and flowerbeds. While 'hortensis' comes from the Latin word for garden, this little mollusk has made itself quite at home wherever humans tend plants, making it both a familiar sight and occasional garden nemesis.
description: The Garden Arion is a small, air-breathing land slug that glides along on its muscular foot, leaving a telltale slime trail behind. These compact slugs typically reach about 1-2 inches long when fully extended, with a rounded back that gives them their family nickname of 'roundback slugs.' Their bodies are soft and squishy to the touch, able to contract dramatically when disturbed, and they breathe through a small breathing pore visible on their right side.

idTips.label: Size and Shape
idTips.description: Small and compact, usually 1-2 inches when crawling, with a distinctly rounded, humped back that feels firm yet squishy when gently touched

idTips.label: Color Pattern
idTips.description: Varies from gray to brown to nearly black, often with darker stripes or bands running lengthwise along the body

idTips.label: Slime Trail
idTips.description: Leaves a clear, sticky mucus trail that feels slippery between your fingers and may have a faint earthy smell

idTips.label: Breathing Pore
idTips.description: Look for a small circular opening on the right side of the body, about one-third back from the head - this pneumostome opens and closes as the slug breathes

idTips.label: Contraction Response
idTips.description: When touched, quickly contracts into a tight, rounded ball, feeling like a firm rubber marble in your palm

habitat: Garden Arions thrive in moist, rich soils throughout New England's gardens, compost piles, and leaf litter. You'll find them hiding under logs, stones, flowerpots, and mulch during the day, especially in areas with good organic matter and consistent moisture. They're particularly common in suburban and urban gardens but also inhabit forest edges and disturbed areas with loose, humus-rich soil.

seasonality.spring: Most active as temperatures warm and moisture increases, emerging from winter hideouts to feed on new plant growth and decomposing organic matter.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity during humid nights and after rain showers, though they hide during hot, dry days under mulch, stones, or in soil crevices.
seasonality.fall: Very active as they feed heavily before winter, often seen on cool, damp mornings moving across garden paths and among fallen leaves.
seasonality.winter: Hidden deep in soil, under logs, or in compost piles in a state of reduced activity, rarely visible unless temperatures rise above freezing for extended periods.

funFact: Garden Arions are hermaphrodites that can literally fence with their reproductive organs - they extend sword-like structures and engage in 'penis fencing' to determine which individual will take on the more energy-expensive role of laying eggs.
confusionNotes: Often confused with other small slugs in gardens, but Garden Arions are distinguished by their ability to contract into a nearly perfect sphere when disturbed - other slugs typically just scrunch up lengthwise. Memory trick: 'Arion balls up like an armadillo.'
contextualKnowledge: The name 'Garden Arion' was historically applied to a complex of several similar species that were later separated by scientists. What we now call the true Garden Arion (Arion hortensis) is just one of several closely related species that were once lumped together under this name, explaining why field guides from different eras might show varying descriptions.
compareHints: Garden Arions are smaller and more compact than their relatives like the Black Slug, which can grow much larger and stays more elongated when disturbed. Unlike the Orange-banded Arion with its distinctive orange stripe, Garden Arions typically show more subdued striping patterns. They're also noticeably smaller than the Western Dusky Slug and contract more completely when threatened than most other Arion species in the region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's Arion slugs, the Western Dusky Slug is one of the smallest and plainest-looking members of its genus.
Among its Arion relatives, the hedgehog slug is most distinctive for its defensive curling behavior - the Black Slug and Garden Arion don't ball up nearly as dramatically.

Black Slugs are the largest and most robust of the Arion genus in New England, with that distinctive rounded back that sets them apart from their smaller, more elongated relatives like the Western Dusky Slug or Garden Arion.
Within the Arion genus, the Northern Dusky Slug is much smaller and more subdued in color compared to the large, jet-black Black Slug or the distinctively marked Orange-banded Arion.

Among its Arion relatives in New England, the Orange-banded Arion is the only one with prominent orange side bands - the Black Slug is uniformly dark, the Garden Arion is typically smaller and grayer, and the Dusky Slugs lack any bright coloration.

Among New England's Arion slugs, the Darkface Arion is most easily distinguished by its characteristic dark facial markings, while the Garden Arion tends to be more uniformly colored and the Black Slug is typically much larger and darker overall.
